newsitem.title: USA: U.S. grain handling mishaps on rise, experts say.
newsitem.headline: U.S. grain handling mishaps on rise, experts say.

text.p: Deaths and serious injuries resulting from handling grain have increased this winter in the U.S. Midwest, and experts said part of the rise was due to grain that has deteriorated in quality since going into storage after the 1996 harvest.

In Kansas alone, one person has died and two others have been seriously injured in the first five weeks of 1997 as a result of grain handling accidents, said John Kramer, agricultural safety specialist at the Kansas State University (KSU) Extension Service in Manhattan, Kan.
Kramer said his records showed there had not been any grain handling fatalities in the state in 1996 or 1995.

A man died Monday after he became engulfed in grain sorghum in an elevator in Alamota, Kan. The state's two other grain-related injuries in 1997 resulted from accidents involving corn and sunflowerseed, Kramer said.
A report released Jan 23 by Purdue University said that since the 1996 corn crop was harvested, at least six people have died in the Midwest after being trapped under grain.
"Most have involved removing grain from storage," the report said.
John Shutske, extension farm safety specialist at the University of Minnesota said seven grain bin fatalities occurred in that state in 1996.
In contrast, the average number of grain-related deaths in the state was just one per year over the past 15 years.
Shutske said there were several possible reasons to explain the "epidemic" in grain bin deaths in 1996.

"The recent harvest was good, resulting in a large amount of grain going into storage again," Shutske said. "However, in many cases the quality is not high, so farmers have (entered) bins more often to check grain quality and unload bins."

KSU's Kramer said it was "not surprising" that accidents were on the rise because high moisture levels and other factors have caused grain quality to deteriorate in some storage bins. Poor quality grain is subject to spoilage, crusting and mold damage, which Kramer said aggravates the dangers of working with stored grain.
"We had a late harvest, and wetter-than-normal grains went into storage. We were set up for storage problems and that's when we really have the risk of accidents," Kramer said.
Most grain bin accidents involve flowing grain, which increases the risk of entrapment and suffocation.

"It only takes about four or five seconds to be caught up and pulled in by flowing grain and less than 20 seconds to go completely under. Grain flows so rapidly that a person pulled in has little chance of escape," Kramer said.
Crusted grain is often as dangerous as flowing grain because breaking the crust can release an avalanche of grain.
There was a similar increase in accidents following the harvest of 1992, which Kramer described as similar to the harvest of 1996 in terms of high mositure levels.
